section_summary: This section chiefly documents preparations for Japan’s April 1946 general election, including candidate lists, campaign conditions, eligibility screening under the occupation purge, Soviet criticism of the election, and Progressive and Liberal Party campaign literature. It also contains a lengthy statement by Wilhelm Classen profiling the wartime Japanese Embassy in Berlin and describing German intelligence personnel, informants, and sources concerned with East Asia. A separate transmittal covers a U.S. Army chart of Japanese ultranationalist societies and their leadership.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 312: Candidates for Japanese Diet
subfiles.from: Officer in Charge, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits copies of the Asahi’s list of announced candidates for the forthcoming Japanese Diet election.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 312 sends Asahi's March 18, 1946 issue with the full list of Diet candidates, untranslated for lack of staff.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 338: Chart of Japanese Ultra-Nationalistic Societies
subfiles.from: Officer in Charge, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits a U.S. Army counterintelligence chart of major Japanese ultranationalist societies.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 338 sends three copies of a counter-intelligence chart of Japanese ultranationalist societies, leaders and affiliations.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 81: Transmitting Statement by Dr. Wilhelm Classen
subfiles.from: C. Orrie, Political Officer, for the U.S. Political Adviser, Frankfurt
subfiles.about: Forwards Wilhelm Classen’s assessment of Far Eastern specialists, the wartime Japanese Embassy in Germany, and German intelligence sources on East Asia.
subfiles.summary: Classen identifies German specialists who might assist a British Far Eastern intelligence section, then supplies detailed political and personal profiles of Ambassador Hiroshi Oshima and other Japanese Embassy officials in wartime Berlin. He emphasizes divisions between Oshima’s strongly pro-Nazi position and more skeptical diplomats, along with Japanese interest in rapprochement with the Soviet Union. A second part surveys German intelligence sources, including the Shanghai station, academics, publishers, Japanese expatriates, cover-name informants, communications interception, Foreign Office reports, Portuguese police contacts, Vlasov officers, and personal access to Asian embassies. The statement names numerous individuals who might still be found in Allied custody or employed as Far Eastern experts.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 343: Political Parties in Japan—Developments During the Week Ending March 30, 1946
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports on campaigning, public interest, party programs, and candidate totals immediately before Japan’s general election.
subfiles.summary: The report finds that campaigning was intensifying despite shortages, travel difficulties, and advertising restrictions, but warns of widespread public apathy and potentially high voter abstention. It attributes this weakness to daily hardship, distrust of politicians, fatalism, limited political education, and ineffective campaigning, and suggests that SCAP encourage voters—especially women—to participate. The report criticizes major-party proposals on inflation, finance, unemployment, and food as vague or inconsistent. As of March 31, it counts 2,787 candidates, including 376 Progressives, 480 Liberals, 330 Social Democrats, 143 Communists, 92 Cooperatives, 564 minor-party candidates, and 802 independents.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1042 from Moscow: Soviet Press Opposition to Japanese Elections
subfiles.to: Secretary of State; repeated to Tokyo and Frankfurt
subfiles.about: Summarizes Soviet newspaper editorials alleging that Japan’s impending election would preserve reactionary and imperialist power.
subfiles.summary: Moscow reports Pravda and Red Fleet say the election's candidates are reactionary and Shidehara's government cannot hold democratic elections; TASS cites New York papers and Berendsen's proposed postponement.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 350 and Translation of Home Affairs Ministry Ordinance No. 2
subfiles.from: Officer in Charge, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the Japanese ordinance establishing certification of election candidates under SCAP’s public-office purge directive.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 350 sends the Official Gazette and translation of Home Affairs Ordinance No. 2 letting candidates seek certification they are not disqualified by SCAP's January 4 purge directive.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 348: Campaign Literature of the Progressive Party
subfiles.from: Max W. Bishop, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Forwards a complete set of Progressive Party campaign materials prepared for its recognized candidates.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 348 sends untranslated Progressive Party campaign literature briefing candidates on the national polity, constitutional revision, inflation, education and food, with model speeches.

subfiles.title: Special Official Gazette Issue: Purge Directive, Candidate Questionnaire, and Certification Forms
subfiles.from: Japanese Home Affairs Ministry and General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Prospective candidates and Japanese government agencies
subfiles.about: Provides the bilingual questionnaire, SCAP removal-and-exclusion directive, disqualification categories, and certification records used to screen candidates and officials.
subfiles.summary: The forms require detailed personal data, employment and military history, organizational memberships, other service, writings, speeches, corporate positions, contributions, honors, and sworn certification. The reproduced SCAP directive orders the removal and exclusion from public office of militarists, ultranationalists, intelligence and police personnel, influential wartime-association officials, and certain executives of expansionist enterprises. It prescribes questionnaires, record cards, reports, inspections, candidate certification, and penalties for false or incomplete disclosure. Appendices enumerate disqualifying military, political, intelligence, colonial, and corporate positions in Japan and occupied territories.

subfiles.title: Despatch No. 351 with Campaign Literature of the Liberal Party
subfiles.from: Officer in Charge, Office of the United States Political Adviser, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits Liberal Party manifestos, emergency programs, constitutional proposals, and a speech by party president Hatoyama for use in the general-election campaign.
subfiles.summary: The enclosed literature declares support for constitutional government, civil liberties, economic freedom, educational reform, the emperor system, women’s political rights, and fulfillment of the Potsdam Declaration. Detailed programs address administration, finance, inflation, food production and imports, agriculture, industry, labor welfare, reconstruction, constitutional revision, and responsibility for wartime profiteering. Emergency proposals call for currency restraint, suspension or postponement of public-debt payments, special taxation of wartime gains and large fortunes, and priority support for essential industries. Hatoyama’s November 9, 1945 founding-convention speech stresses the food crisis, democratic reconstruction, defense of the emperor and private property, and opposition to communist dictatorship; the speech continues beyond page 548.
